Charlotte Brontë. Eighteen eighteen to eighteen forty-eight. A British novelist whose Jane Eyre became a cornerstone of English literature, pioneering the female bildungsroman and the depiction of female independence. Born in Yorkshire to an Irish clergyman's family, she and her siblings—including the similarly gifted Emily and Anne—created a rich imaginative world that fueled their later published works.

She wrote under the pseudonym Currer Bell to bypass contemporary prejudice against female authors. Jane Eyre in eighteen forty-seven broke convention by centering a poor, plain, ordinary heroine who speaks her mind, resists patriarchal authority, and demands respect and equality in love. She incorporated gothic elements—the mysterious laugh in the attic, the burning of Thornfield—into a deeply introspective psychological narrative. Her heroine refuses to become a kept woman or a missionary's dutiful wife. She insists on marriage based on mutual respect and equality.

Brontë also authored The Professor, published posthumously, which drew on her experience as a governess in Belgium. She died at thirty, likely from complications of pregnancy, leaving a relatively small but enormously influential body of work. Her upbringing in isolated Yorkshire moorland and her creative collaboration with her siblings shaped her imaginative power and her unflinching treatment of isolation and intensity.

Jane Eyre was initially controversial for its passionate language, its heroine's refusal to be submissive, and its suggestion that female desire and agency were as legitimate as male experience.
